p: Students' Learning Outcomes:
At the end of this unit, students will be able to:
Students' Learning Outcomes:

recognize cells as the basic unit of life that are organized into tissues, organs, systems and organisms. • arrange and rank different levels of cellular organizations – cells to tissues, organs, organs system and organisms. • relate the structures of some common cells (nerve, muscle, epithelium and blood cells) to their functions.
Students' Learning Outcomes:

• identify the structures present in an animal cell and plant cell as seen under a simple microscope and relate them to their functions (only cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, cell wall, chloroplast, mitochondria and vacuole). • describe the similarities and differences between the structures of plant and animal cells. • sketch the animal and plant cells and label key organelles in each.
Students' Learning Outcomes:
• compare and contrast an animal cell and plant cell by preparing slides using onion peels and cheek cells.
Students' Learning Outcomes:
Can you identify something which is common in all of the following picture?
Students' Learning Outcomes:
Yes. All of these are living things. All living things share some characteristics;
Students' Learning Outcomes:

They need food. • They grow with the passage of time. • They produce wastes and excrete them. • They can move towards or away from things. • They are sensitive to changes in their surroundings and they respond to these changes. • They reproduce for the continuity of life. • They respire to release energy from food. • They are made up of cells.
Figure 1.1 Living things
Photographs of a lizard, mushrooms, a beetle, forest trees, a fern and daisies.
1.1 CELL

Do you know that your body is made up of trillions of tiny living units? In every given minute many of these units are formed, some die and many continue to do their jobs. Do you know what they are called?
1.1 CELL

Cells are the building blocks of our bodies. All living things are made of these tiny living units, called cells. A cell is so small in size that you cannot see at it simply with your naked eyes. You need microscope to observe a cell.
1.1 CELL

Organisms may be unicellular or multicellular. Unicellular organisms are made up of one cell, for example, bacteria, amoeba etc. Multicellular organisms consists of many cells, for example, rose, frog etc. Animals and plants are made up of many cells and are, therefore, called multicellular organisms.
DO YOU KNOW?

Cells were discovered after the invention of microscope. The cell was first discovered and named by Robert Hooke in 1665. He observed a thin slice of a cork under a microscope and noticed small boxes surrounded by walls, which he named as cells.
INTERESTING FACTS
Microscope is one of the basic tools of a scientist. It is an instrument used to see small things. The apparent size of an object magnifies when observed under microscope.
Onion membrane slide preparation
A thin onion membrane • Microscopic glass slides • Microscopic cover slips • Needle • Dropper • Methylene blue solution • Water • Microscope
Onion membrane slide preparation

Procedure: Carefully cut a piece of thin onion membrane. Put a piece of this tissue on glass slide. Straighten it with the help of needle. Add a drop of Methylene blue solution to it and put a cover slip on it. Methylene blue is a stain that helps to observe cells. Observe under microscope. Draw and label what you see.
Onion membrane slide preparation
Checklist of observations
Onion membrane slide preparation

Large, rectangular interlocking cells • Clearly visible distinct cell walls surrounding the cells • Dark stained nucleus • Large vacuoles at the center • Small granules may be observed inside the cells (within the cytoplasm)
Cheek cell slide preparation
Sterile, individually packed cotton swabs • Microscopic glass slides • Microscopic cover slips • Needle • Dropper • Methylene blue solution • Water • Microscope
Cheek cell slide preparation

Take a clean cotton swab and gently scrape the inside of your cheek. • Smear the cotton swab on the centre of the microscope slide for 2 to 3 seconds. • Add a drop of methylene blue solution and place a coverslip on top. • Remove any excess solution by allowing a paper towel to touch one side of the coverslip. • Methylene blue stains nucleus of the cell.
Cheek cell slide preparation

This dye is toxic when ingested and it causes irritation when in contact with the skin and eyes. • The cells seen are squamous epithelial cells from the outer epithelial layer of the mouth. The small blue dots are bacteria from our teeth and mouth.
Cell Structure

All living things are made up of basic units called cells. Here we will learn about the cells present in animals and plants. If we look at an animal and a plant cell under a microscope, we can see similarities and differences between them.
DO YOU KNOW?

Your body has about 75 trillion cells. • Some of your nerve cells can live throughout your life. • Some white blood cells and intestine cells live only for 3 days. • Ostrich egg is the largest cell in the world. • It would take about 200 of your cells to fit on a full stop.
Similarities between an Animal and a Plant Cell
Many parts of the cell are same in both animals and plants. Both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus.
Similarities between an Animal and a Plant Cell
Cell membrane is a thin, protective layer around a cell. It holds all parts of the cell together. It is the boundary with pores to control what moves in and out of the cell.
Similarities between an Animal and a Plant Cell
Nucleus acts as the control center of the cell. It contains all information of the cell in its thread like structures called chromosomes.
Similarities between an Animal and a Plant Cell

Cytoplasm is a watery gel which fills the space between the cell membrane and the nucleus. All essential functions of the cell are performed in the cytoplasm. Cytoplasm contains many small structures called organelles.
Similarities between an Animal and a Plant Cell
Cell organelles perform different jobs for the cell. There are many types of organelles in a cell. Some are common in both animal and plant cells, for example, mitochondria
Similarities between an Animal and a Plant Cell

(singular: mitochondrion), ribosomes etc. Mitochondria break down the food to release energy and are therefore called the power house of the cell. Ribosomes are very small organelles which are the factories of protein.
Differences between Animal and Plant Cell
Some of the differences between an animal cell and a plant cell are as follows.
Differences between Animal and Plant Cell

Cell wall is present outside the cell membrane of a plant cell. It is a hard and dead layer made up of cellulose. Cellulose is a large molecule which we cannot digest. It is a natural fiber found in plants. When we eat plants, the fiber acts like a broom to clean our intestines. Cell wall gives the plant cell a fixed shape. Animal cell is without cell wall.
Differences between Animal and Plant Cell

Chloroplast is a special organelle for photosynthesis, found in the green parts of a plant. It contains a green pigment called chlorophyll. Chloroplast absorbs sunlight, carbon dioxide and water to make food and oxygen. It is not present in animal cell.
Differences between Animal and Plant Cell

Vacuole stores different types of substances like water and salts if in abundance. Plant cells have a large central vacuole. A fluid filled vacuole provides support from inside to the plant cell. It increases in size during plant growth. Animal cell has small vacuoles dispersed in the cytoplasm.
Animal or plant cell model (Group work)
Make a model of animal or plant cell, using materials of your choice. Label its parts.
Types of Cells
There are many types of cells. Few examples are discussed here.
Types of Cells

Animal cells | Function | Special features; Red blood cell | transport oxygen from lungs to different parts of the body | large surface area for oxygen absorption; contains haemoglobin, which combines with oxygen; Nerve cell | carry messages all around the body | very long and thin; connections at each end; can carry messages in the form of electrical signals
Types of Cells

Animal cells | Function | Special features; Muscle cell | work by contracting and relaxing to move different parts of the body | long, thin cells grouped into bundles; many mitochondria present; Epithelium cells | protection, coverage, secretion, excretion, absorption, and filtration. | tightly packed sheets of cells; present on the body surfaces and inner cavities
1.3 TISSUE
A group of similar cells performing a specific function is called a tissue. Animal tissues are broadly classified into four groups.
1.3 TISSUE

Animal Tissues | Function | Where it is found; Epithelial Tissue | covers, protects and secretes | skin, lining of tubes and organs; Connective Tissue | connects, transports and supports | bone, blood, cartilage, fats, loose connective tissues etc.; Muscular Tissue | moves body parts | heart, muscles etc.; Nervous Tissue | carries messages around the body | brain, spinal cord and nerves
1.3 TISSUE

Plant Tissues | Function | Where it is found; Epidermal Tissue | covers and protects | surface of leaves, stem and roots; Photosynthetic Tissue | makes food | green leaves; Supporting Tissue | supports and strengthens | wood of stem and root; Vascular Tissue | moves water and food | vascular bundles (xylem and phloem)
1.4 ORGAN

Tissues join with other tissues to form an organ. Different tissues of an organ work together to do a special job. For example, stomach is an organ to digest food. Epithelial tissue, muscular tissue, blood tissue and nerve tissue join to form an organ e.g stomach.
1.5 ORGAN SYSTEM

A group of organs work together to carry out a life process. For example, in your body 206 bones make up the skeletal system. This system provides support to your body, protects your internal organs and helps you move.
1.5 ORGAN SYSTEM

The circulatory system moves blood around the body to transport digested food, oxygen, carbon dioxide, waste material, heat etc. The muscular system works with bones to help the body move. The digestive system breaks down food into simpler substances.
1.5 ORGAN SYSTEM

The respiratory system provides oxygen to the blood and removes carbon dioxide. The nervous system controls all activities of the body. The excretory system removes waste from the body. The skeletal system supports the body and protects delicate organs and helps in movement.
Teaching Point:
Teacher will explain that all these systems coordinate together for normal working of the human body.
1.6 ORGANISM
All organ systems work together to make a complex organism. An organism is able to survive on its own.
Key Points

Cell is the structural and functional unit of living things. • Some structures are common in a plant and an animal cell e.g. cell membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria and ribosome. • Some structures are present only in plant cell e.g. cell wall, chloroplast and large central vacuole. • Cells form tissue, tissues form organs, organs form system and organ systems form an organism.
Key Points
• All organ systems work in coordination with each other to perform the life processes.
Students' Learning Outcomes:
At the end of this unit, students will be able to:
Students' Learning Outcomes:

describe the different types of reproduction in plants. • compare and contrast types of reproduction (sexual and asexual) in plants. • distinguish between artificial and natural asexual reproduction in plants. (budding, bulbs, tuber, runners, cutting, grafting, and layering.) • inquire how artificial propagation can lead to better quality yield in agriculture.
2.1 REPRODUCTION IN PLANTS

You learned about some life processes in previous unit. One of them is reproduction. The process of producing new organisms from their parents is called reproduction. Reproduction ensures that a group of organisms does not disappear from Earth. This process is very important for the continuation of life on Earth.
2.1 REPRODUCTION IN PLANTS
Plants reproduce by two ways i.e., sexual reproduction and asexual reproduction.
DO YOU KNOW?

The parts of the plants can be divided into two groups i.e., reproductive and vegetative parts. Reproductive part includes only flower, while all other plant parts are called vegetative parts including root, stem and leaves.
2.2 SEXUAL REPRODUCTION

Do you like to grow plants? Have you grown any seedling? All flowering plants can be grown from seeds. Sexual reproduction involves the fusion of male and female gametes. The male gametes are inside pollen grain and female gametes are present in ovule. Do you remember structure of flower from grade 4? Sexual reproduction takes place in flowers.
2.2 SEXUAL REPRODUCTION
It includes gamete formation, pollination, fertilization, seed formation and seed dispersal.
2.3 ASEXUAL REPRODUCTION

Have you grown any cutting of plant? Can you grow plants without using seeds? Asexual reproduction involves formation of new plants from vegetative parts like root, stem and leaves. This type of reproduction is also called vegetative propagation. It does not require flower or seed formation.
Teaching Point:
Clones are genetically identical organisms. Vegetative propagation produces natural clones in the form of crops quickly, easily, at low cost and with less water requirement.
DO YOU KNOW?

Asexual reproduction produces organisms identical to their parents called clones. While sexual reproduction creates new varieties. Can you identify which field of tulip is produced by asexual reproduction?
Pictures A and B
"A": a field of tulips that are all the same orange colour. "B": a field of tulips of many mixed colours (orange, red, pink, white, yellow).
2.3 ASEXUAL REPRODUCTION
There are many types of asexual reproduction. This propagation can be classified into two main types i.e., natural and artificial.
2.4 NATURAL PROPAGATION OF PLANTS
Many plants reproduce through vegetative propagation naturally. Methods of natural propagation include budding, bulbs, tuber and runners.
DO YOU KNOW?
A bud is a small swelling that can grow into new branches, leaves or flowers. In vegetative propagation, roots and shoots grow from buds. New plants are formed from these buds.
Budding
Juicy leaf plants like Air plant have buds at the margins of their leaves. Each bud develops into a new plant. Air plant is also called "Zakhm-e-Hayat".
Bulb
A bulb is a type of an underground stem with thick, fleshy leaves that store food. It produces smaller buds which grow into new plants.
Tuber
It is a swollen, underground stem. Each bud can be cut and planted to grow into a new plant.
Runner
Runners are plant stems that run along the ground. New strawberry plants grow from the buds along the runners of the parent strawberry plant.
2.5 ARTIFICIAL VEGETATIVE PROPAGATION
Artificial vegetative propagation requires human action. The most common types of artificial vegetative reproductive techniques include cutting, layering, grafting etc.
Cutting
A stem cutting from a rose plant will grow roots and form a new plant. Root and leaf cuttings can also be grown.
Layering
When a branch of shrub touches the ground, it produces roots and forms a new plant. Layering can be done by bending a branch, removing a ring of bark and covering it with the soil.
Grafting

Grafting is a technique of combining two plants. It uses the roots and the bottom portion of one plant (rootstock) and attach it to shoot (scion) from the top portion of another plant. Grafting is done for many fruit trees.
2.6 ADVANTAGES OF VEGETATIVE PROPAGATION
Agriculture specially fruits trees growth depends on the benefits of the vegetative propagation. The desirable plants can be reproduced exactly, quickly and cheaply by these methods.
2.6 ADVANTAGES OF VEGETATIVE PROPAGATION
Following are the benefits of vegetative propagation.
2.6 ADVANTAGES OF VEGETATIVE PROPAGATION

Quick and easy way to produce new plants • New plants are identical to the parent plant • Desirable fruit characters are maintained • Only one parent is required for reproduction, so there is no need of pollination etc. • Plants that do not produce seeds are propagated by these methods, for example banana
2.6 ADVANTAGES OF VEGETATIVE PROPAGATION
There are some disadvantages as well such as:
2.6 ADVANTAGES OF VEGETATIVE PROPAGATION
No new variety can be produced • Cannot cope with changing environmental conditions • Very little chance of surviving any disease attack

Key Points

It increases the number of identical plants in a short period of time. • Natural vegetative propagation techniques include budding, bulbs, tuber and runners.
Key Points
• Artificial vegetative propagation techniques include cutting, grafting, layering etc. • Agriculture is improved by the use of artificial vegetative propagation.

4.1 DIGESTION

You just learned that your food mainly consists of large molecules of carbohydrates, proteins and fats. These molecules are too big to enter your cells through cell membrane. 4.1 DIGESTION

Digestion begins as soon as you chew the food. It continues as the food travels through the organs of the digestive system. Food breakdown starts with physical digestion. The large pieces of food are broken into smaller pieces by cutting and chewing action of your teeth. Your tongue also helps by mixing and rolling of food. The muscles of your stomach help in mechanical digestion.

4.1 DIGESTION

Rest of the digestion is chemical digestion by enzymes. Digestive enzymes breakdown large food molecules into smaller molecules. For example, the bread you eat has large molecules which are broken by enzymes into smaller molecules. These small molecules are absorbed and used by the cells.
4.2 HUMAN DIGESTIVE SYSTEM

1. Digestion begins in mouth: Physical digestion by Teeth (tearing and crushing) and Tongue (rolling and mixing). Chemical digestion by enzymes of saliva (for starch digestion). • 2. The food you swallow enters a food pipe called oesophagus. Smooth muscles in its walls contract and push the food towards stomach. • 3. The partly digested food enters your stomach:
4.2 HUMAN DIGESTIVE SYSTEM

Physical digestion by smooth muscles in the walls (churning). Chemical digestion by gastric juice from stomach glands. It has enzymes and acid for protein digestion. After several hours in the stomach the food becomes a soupy mixture. Muscles push this thick liquid into the small intestine. • Liver produces bile to help fat digestion. Gall bladder stores bile.
4.2 HUMAN DIGESTIVE SYSTEM

Pancreas produces digestive enzymes that flow into small intestine. • 4. Chemical digestion completes in the small intestine. Enzymes from pancreas and intestinal glands digest all types of food into nutrients. These nutrients are absorbed into the blood through the walls of the villi. Villi are tiny finger like projections lining the small intestine. • 5.
4.2 HUMAN DIGESTIVE SYSTEM

Materials that cannot be digested and some liquids move into large intestine. It absorbs water from the undigested material. No digestion takes place here. • 6. Rectum stores the solid waste called faeces until it leaves the body through anus.

5.2 PARTICLE THEORY OF MATTER

All matter is made up of small particles. There are spaces in the particles and they are in constant motion. Based on the arrangement of the particles, matter can exist in different states. Books, chairs, tables, your school bag are all solids. Similarly, water or the drink in your water bottle is liquid and the air around you is an example of gas.
Teaching Point:

Solids
Arrangement of particles in a solid state
Solids

The particles in the solid are tightly packed together. • The forces of attraction between the particles are very strong. • The tightly packed particles of the solids give them a definite shape. • It is hard to compress solids. • More energy is required to break the forces of attraction in the particles of a solid.
Solids

Example: A book has a certain shape, but can you squeeze a book into your pencil box? Or your chair in your school bag? Obviously not! You need a school bag of a certain size to ensure it fills in all your books, notebooks, lunch box and pencil box because all solids have a certain shape that occupies the space accordingly.
Solids
Similarly, wood and metals are other examples of hard solids which cannot be compressed and retain their original shapes.
Solids
More examples are shown below: a) Metallic nail b) Wood c) Table and chair d) Books
Liquids
Arrangement of particles in a liquid state
Liquids

The particles in liquids are close together but not very tightly packed as in solids. • The particles of the liquids are continuously moving and sliding onto one another. • Liquids don't have a definite shape and they acquire the shape of container. • Liquids have weak attractive forces between their particles. This allows particles to slide past one another, so liquids can flow.
Liquids
• It is not easier to compress liquids, like solids. • Less energy is required to overcome the force of attraction between the particles of liquids as compared to solids.
Liquids
Liquids: Oil, Mercury, Water, Milk, Blood

5.4 CHANGES IN STATES OF MATTER

You may have seen changes in the state of matter, but have you ever thought of why or how such changes occur in their form? When any form of matter gains or loses energy, the condition changes. In this chapter we will refer to this energy as Heat energy. When a substance gains energy, internal changes occur.
5.4 CHANGES IN STATES OF MATTER

Molecules or atoms start moving faster, and particles are pushed at a sufficient distance apart from each other, which results in their shape change. While the opposite occurs when heat energy is lost, particles start coming together, and movement of the particles becomes slower, steady at their respective positions.

5.4 CHANGES IN STATES OF MATTER

Physical changes in matter are known as the changes in their condition. All these changes are reversible changes, meaning, they can be brought back to their original conditions. These changes are brought by different processes, shown in figure.
5.4 CHANGES IN STATES OF MATTER
1) Freezing and Melting 2) Evaporation and Condensation 3) Sublimation (naphthalene solid → gas)
Change of phase between solids and liquids

How do you form ice at home? Refrigerators often have freezer compartments, which include an ice tray. To begin the process, water is poured into the ice tray, which is then cooled by placing it into the freezer compartment. So, what happens next? The process is shown in figure 5.8.
Change of phase between solids and liquids

Freezing: Our surrounding environment is warmer in comparison to the freezer's cooler air. The warm water placed inside the freezer loses heat to the cold air inside. The heat transfer occurs continuously, resulting in the particles to lose their energy, resulting in no energy for them to freely move. The particles are brought closer to each other, and they are forced to remain in their fixed place.
Change of phase between solids and liquids
Water (liquid) is then transformed into Ice(solid). The process is known as freezing.
Change of phase between solids and liquids

Melting: Now, if the ice cubes are removed from the freezer and kept outside in the air, which we discussed previously to be warmer than the cold air inside the freezer, the ice cubes will absorb heat from the warmer air. This heat gain breaks the bonds of the particles of the solid, the molecules start moving faster pushing each other at some distances apart. Ice (solid) is transformed into water (liquid).
Change of phase between solids and liquids
The process is known as melting. An example can be seen in figure.
Change of phase between gases and liquids

Tea is enjoyed in almost every household, but what do we do first? We pour cold water in our pot, and then put the pot on the stove to heat it up. Heat energy is absorbed by the water, but what happens to the water after that?
Change of phase between gases and liquids

Evaporation: When the water is heated, it is converted into vapours which indicates evaporation. Notice: If you ever place your hand at a safe distance from the pot, you can feel your hands becoming watery. Once water is heated, water vapours are formed.
Change of phase between gases and liquids

This is because the water particles have gained heat energy, which results in particle motion, they start moving faster and push the particles further apart than they already are. The bubbles of water vapour rise and exit as steam (which we can feel on our hands). Water (liquid) is transformed into steam/ water vapours (gas). The process is known as evaporation. Shown in the figure 5.10:
Change of phase between gases and liquids

Condensation: Have you ever noticed the fog on the mirror when you take a hot shower in a closed bathroom? It might have made you curious as to why this happens. The hot water in the shower evaporates as we previously learnt. It then cools down and loses energy when it comes in contact with colder surfaces such as the bathroom mirror. As a result, the particles come closer together forming water droplets.
Change of phase between gases and liquids
Water vapours (gas) formed because of evaporation, are transformed to water droplets (liquid). The process is known as condensation.

8.1 ENERGY

Energy is used for performing many day-to-day tasks. We need it for transportation, running the fans and lights at home and for watching our favourite shows on TV. It is also used on a larger scale in industries and factories for manufacturing different products. Scientists define energy as, "the ability to do work". Work is done when a force causes movement of an object.
8.1 ENERGY

8.2 CATEGORIES OF ENERGY

Energy exists in different forms like heat, light, sound, electrical, thermal etc. but interesting point is that all energy types can be classified into two categories i.e Kinetic energy and Potential energy.
1. KINETIC ENERGY (KE):
Energy of a body due to its motion is called kinetic energy. It can be in the form of heat, light, sound, electricity or motion of any object.
1. KINETIC ENERGY (KE):

In above figures, truck is in state of rest so its kinetic energy is zero while horses are running so they have kinetic energy. When the truck will move, its kinetic energy will increase. It means that when truck starts motion its kinetic energy increases gradually, with the increase of its speed.
1. KINETIC ENERGY (KE):
Kinetic energy also depends upon mass of an object, for example a truck has more kinetic energy as compared to a car moving at the same speed, because truck has more mass as compare to car.
2. POTENTIAL ENERGY (PE):

Energy possessed by a body due to its position is called potential energy. It can be in the form of stored energy, gravitational potential energy (GPE) or elastic potential energy (EPE). When something is at high position, its GPE is greater e.g., a brick lying on the roof of a house has greater GPE as compared to brick lying on the ground.
2. POTENTIAL ENERGY (PE):
EPE is the energy stored in something when you push, pull or force it out of shape e.g., a stretched bow has EPE. In batteries, energy is stored in the form of chemical energy.

8.3 CONVERSION OF ENERGY

Think of a book lying on a shelf. The book has potential energy when it is on the shelf. What happens if the book falls off the shelf? Its potential energy changes into kinetic energy. This change in energy from one form to another is transformation of energy. In conversion total amount of energy remains constant.
Transformation of energy
What are the Energy Changes when a Ball Bounces?
Transformation of energy
By the help of this example of bouncing ball, we can study the transformation of energies from one form to another form. There are 4-different stages of energy changes.
Transformation of energy
STAGE-1: At height 'h' ball has GPE. When it drops, its GPE converts into kinetic energy due to its motion.
Transformation of energy

STAGE-2: Due to kinetic energy ball moves down and hits the ground. As it hits the ground it changes the shape of ball. Here kinetic energy is converted to EPE. Here some kinetic energy is lost as heat energy and sound energy.
Transformation of energy
STAGE-3: EPE is converted into kinetic energy. As a result the ball bounces back to height 'h'.
Transformation of energy
STAGE-4: Due to kinetic energy ball will move up and will reach height 'h'. Kinetic energy will be converted into potential energy.
Transformation of energy

CONCLUSION: From above example we can conclude that energy can be converted into any other form of energy but total energy remains conserved. If the energy transfers were perfect and there were no energy losses, the bouncing ball would always return to the same height at which it started. It would carry on bouncing like this forever.

8.6 ENERGY SOURCES

Energy is the capacity to do work and is required for life processes. An energy resource is something that can produce heat, move objects, or produce electricity. Matter that stores energy is called a fuel. Human energy consumption has grown steadily throughout human history. Early humans had less energy requirements, mostly food and fuel for fires to cook and keep warm.
8.6 ENERGY SOURCES

In today's society, humans consume as much as 110 times more energy per person as compared to early humans. Most of the energy we use today come from fossil fuels. But fossils fuels have a disadvantage in that they are non-renewable on a human time scale, and cause other potentially harmful effects on the environment.
8.7 RENEWABLE ENERGY SOURCES

Renewable energy comes from sources or processes that are constantly replenished. These sources do not run out and are naturally recycled. For example, solar energy, wind energy, geothermal energy, hydroelectric energy and energy of biomass.
8.7 RENEWABLE ENERGY SOURCES

Solar Energy: Sunlight can produce electrical energy by using a photovoltaic cell. They are usually arranged in frames known as solar panels. This is a free and unlimited source of energy. However, its effectiveness is determined by the number of hours of daylight, cloud and weather conditions.
8.7 RENEWABLE ENERGY SOURCES
Wind Energy: Wind turbines turn wind into electrical energy. Sites for wind farms are chosen carefully in the windy regions to effectively generate electricity.
8.7 RENEWABLE ENERGY SOURCES
Hydroelectric Energy: Hydroelectric energy generates electricity from flowing water using turbines and other devices. It is renewable and can be generated from rivers or dams.
8.7 RENEWABLE ENERGY SOURCES
Biomass Energy: Biomass is renewable energy material that comes from plants and animals. It can be used as fuel to produce heat or electricity e.g., biodiesel, biogas plant etc.
8.7 RENEWABLE ENERGY SOURCES

Geothermal Energy: As the core of the earth is hot, we can use its geothermal energy to generate electricity. This energy is accessible just a few kilometers below the earth's surface in some parts of the world.
8.8 NON-RENEWABLE ENERGY SOURCES

Non-renewable energy source comes from natural sources that does not replenish quickly. These sources typically take millions of years to develop. Fossil fuels and nuclear energy are non-renewable energy sources. This means that they will run out eventually, that is why their cost is increasing. Coal, oil and natural gas are examples of fossil fuels.
8.8 NON-RENEWABLE ENERGY SOURCES

They are burnt to generate electricity, however, carbon dioxide is released during this process. Carbon dioxide contributes to global warming. Both fossil fuels and nuclear energy are harmful for the environment. Burning of fossil fuels cause air pollution, global warming, smog and acid rain.

9.1 STATIC ELECTRICITY

Some objects can be charged by rubbing, like in winter season, when we sleep in the wool blanket; it gets charged by rubbing with our body and after some time when we touch the blanket it gives tiny sparks. Objects acquire charges when they are rubbed with any other object. For example, when you use a plastic comb in your dry hair it becomes negatively charged while your hair gets positive charge.
9.1 STATIC ELECTRICITY

Your hair repel each other as they have the same charge. Rubbing two bodies together cannot have same charges on both bodies. On rubbing, bodies become charged as electrons transfer from one body to another. Electrons has some mass (although negligible). So with transfer of charge, some mass is also transferred. Therefore, mass of each body changes slightly.
9.1 STATIC ELECTRICITY
Since mass is transferred from one body to another, it is not lost anywhere else, so total mass remains same.

10.1 MAGNETIC FIELD

You learned about magnets and the properties of magnets in grade 5. A region around the magnet where a force acts on other magnets or magnetic materials is called magnetic field. Magnetic field lines are invisible but they can be displayed by using iron filings or magnetic compass. Place a paper on a bar magnet. Sprinkle iron filings on this paper.
10.1 MAGNETIC FIELD

Iron filings will display the magnetic field in the form of magnetic field lines. Iron filings set themselves in a pattern because of magnetic field created by the magnet. Within a bar magnet, to a very good approximation, the magnetic field lines point from North to South (where N and S are the two respective poles of the bar magnet).
10.1 MAGNETIC FIELD

Magnetic lines of force always forms closed loops. The direction of magnetic field lines can be determined by using magnetic compass. These field lines seem to originate from the North pole (N) and end into the South pole (S) of a bar magnet outside the magnet and from South to North inside the magnet.
Formation of magnetic field

Plot the magnetic field lines of a bar magnet using a plotting compass. Magnetic field lines do not ever cross, they are continuous, and they go from North to South. The closer these lines are, the stronger the magnetic field it represents. Magnetic field lines can be plotted, and their direction can be determined by using a magnetic compass.
Formation of magnetic field

Method: Place the bar magnet in the middle of the paper. Put the magnetic compass next to one of the poles, and put a pencil dot where the compass points. Move the compass so that the tail end of the pointer aims at that dot. Again, put a pencil dot where the compass points. Repeat until the compass returns to the other pole. Join up the dots. Add arrows to show that the field points from the N pole to the S pole.
Formation of magnetic field
Repeat from another starting point.

10.3 MAGNETIC FIELD AROUND A CONDUCTOR

Electric current produces a magnetic field around it. When we pass current through a straight wire, a circular magnetic field lines are produced. The magnetic field lines are concentric circles with common centre of the wire. This can be verified by using a compass needle.

Permanent Magnet

A permanent magnet retains its magnetic properties in the absence of any other magnet or current. It produces its own magnetic field. Permanent magnets are made from special alloys having iron, nickel and cobalt,
Temporary Magnet

Temporary magnets are those that simply act like magnets when they are within a strong magnetic field. They lose their magnetic properties in the absence of any other magnet or current. These are made of soft iron.
Electromagnet
An electromagnet is a type of magnet in which the magnetic field is produced by an electric current. The magnetic field disappears when the current is turned off.
Electromagnet

When current passes through the coil around the steel nail, a magnetic field will be developed around it. So it will start to behave like electromagnet. When flow of charges through the coil stops then the developed magnetic field around it will also be vanished. It means that this magnet will behave like a temporary magnet.

10.6 HOW TO MAGNETIZE A MAGNETIC MATERIAL?

Temporary magnets do not have their own magnetic field. There are several methods to magnetize magnetic materials. The most commonly used are single touch or double touch method and electrical method.
10.6 HOW TO MAGNETIZE A MAGNETIC MATERIAL?

When a magnet is rubbed along the magnetic material like needle or iron piece from one end to another end lifted vertically upwards such method is called single touch method of magnetization. While when opposite poles of two magnets are placed next to each other at the center of the magnetic substance and rubbed in opposite directions, such method is called double touch method of magnetization.
10.6 HOW TO MAGNETIZE A MAGNETIC MATERIAL?
In electrical method a bar of steel can be magnetized by placing it in a coil of wire. When current from batteries will pass through the coil, bar will be magnetized.
10.7 DEMAGNETIZATION
Demagnetization is the process of removing the magnetic field from an object. Demagnetization occurs naturally over time. Three methods are very common to demagnetize the magnetic substances.
Heating
When temporary magnets are heated at high temperature on a burner they lose their magnetic strength.
Hammering
Repeated hammering weakens the magnetic strength of a magnet. Similarly dropping magnets on hard surface can result in demagnetization.
Electrical Method
If a bar magnet is pushed in a coil of wire and the ends of the wire are connected to alternating current, then it can demagnetize the bar magnet.

Pour the half liter milk in a large saucepan. • Bring the milk to boil. • Turn the heat down to low. • While stirring the milk continuously, pour one table spoon of vinegar or lemon juice. • The milk will curdle, meaning that the milk fat (curds) separates from the liquid in the milk (whey). • Allow the milk to cool slightly.
Direction

• Separate the whey from curd using cheese cloth or strainer • Gently roll the curds up in the cheese cloth. • Place the cheese cloth on a draining board and allow the cheese to drain for two hours. • You can also hang the cloth until all the water drips down.
Direction
Enjoy. Place any uneaten cheese in the refrigerator. It is best to use the cheese within three days

12.1 PLANETS
Any relatively large natural body that revolves in an orbit around the Sun or around some other star is called planet.
12.1 PLANETS

As of June 2013, approximately 900 planets have been identified in the universe. In our solar system, there are eight planets, listed in order of proximity to the Sun, they are: (i) Mercury (ii) Venus (iii) Earth (iv) Mars (v) Jupiter (vi) Saturn (vii) Uranus and (viii) Neptune
Inner planets (Terrestrial planets)
The closet planets to the sun are called inner planets. These are mainly made of rocks namely Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.
Outer planets (Gas giants)
The planets which are far away from the sun are called outer planets. These are mostly composed of gas namely Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
Teaching Point
Teach students the planets of our solar system starting with the planet closest to the Sun, Mercury. It is best to teach children the planets in order.

Comparison of Earth and other Planet's days and years according to Earth time

Planets | Period of rotation (One day) | Period of revolution (One year); Mercury | 59 days | 88 days; Venus | 243 days | 225 days; Earth | 24 hours | 365 days; Mars | 25 hours | 687 days; Jupiter | 10 hours | 12 years; Saturn | 10 hours | 29 years; Uranus | 18 hours | 84 years; Neptune | 19 hours | 165 years
Information

Jupiter has a diameter of about 88,695 miles (142,800 kilometers) which is more than 11 times the diameter of Earth. Its volume is over 1,300 times the volume of Earth. This means that Jupiter is so big that over 1,300 Earths could fit inside of it.
DO YOU KNOW?

Jupiter is the largest planet in the Solar System. Its diameter is about 11 times the diameter of Earth. • Mercury is the smallest planet of solar system. 18 Mercury planets can fit into Earth. • Venus is the hottest and Neptune is the coldest planet. • Venus rotates so slowly on its axis that its one day is almost equal to one year of the Earth.
Planets

The Sun and the cluster of bodies around it make up our Solar System. Our Earth is one of the eight planets in the Solar System of our Sun. These planets revolve around the Sun in fixed orbits that are almost circular. The gravity of the Sun holds all the planets in their orbits. Some planets have one or more moons.
Planets
In 2006, the International Astronomical Union (IAU) defined a planet as having the following three essential criteria:
Planets

1. A celestial object that revolves around a star. • 2. It is large enough that its gravity pulls it into the shape of a sphere. • 3. It must be big enough that its gravity cleared away any other objects of a similar size near its orbit around the Sun.
Dwarf Planets

In addition to the eight planets there are other celestial bodies in the solar system that revolve around the Sun. Some of them are much smaller than the eight planets and hence are not classified as full-fledged planets. These are called the dwarf planets. There are five dwarf planets in the solar system. These are the same as normal planets, just smaller.
Dwarf Planets
Dwarf planets are natural objects outside of Earth's atmosphere that:
Dwarf Planets
revolve around the Sun • have enough mass so that their gravity pulls them to be nearly round • are not moons • share their pathway with other outer space objects
12.4 ASTEROIDS, METEORITES AND COMETS
Asteroids, Meteorites and Comets are small solar system bodies. They are not visible from Earth with the naked eye but many may be seen through binoculars or small telescopes.
Asteroid:
Asteroid is an object larger than a meteoroid that revolves around the Sun and is made of rock or metal.
Asteroid:
Let's discuss the main characteristics of Asteroids:
Asteroid:

Asteroids are also called minor planets or planetoids, any of a host of small bodies, which orbit the Sun between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter in a nearly flat ring called the asteroid belt. • They are rocky objects with either round or irregular shapes. • Some of them are several hundred kilometers across while others are much smaller.
Asteroid:
• Scientists think that this debris may be the remains of an early planet, which broke up early in the solar system.
Meteorite:

A meteorite is a solid piece of debris from an object, such as a comet, asteroid, or meteoroid, which originates in outer space. It survives its passage through the atmosphere to reach the surface of Earth.
Meteorite:
Let's discuss the main characteristics of Meteoroids:
Meteorite:

Meteoroids are pieces of rocks or irons that are found in the Solar System. • Their size ranges from a few millimeters to thousands of kilometers in diameter. • When they enter the Earth's atmosphere they become incandescent as a result of friction and appear as a streak of light and splash across the sky. • We sometimes call it a falling star.
Comets:
Comets are a body of ice, rock and dust that can be several miles in diameter and revolve around the Sun. Let's discuss the main characteristics of Comets:
Comets:

Comets are celestial bodies mostly made up of rock and dust stuck together with ice and gases. • Sometimes light from the Sun hits the gases and is reflected to give a glowing tail millions of kilometer long. • Comets grow new tails each time they get close to the Sun. • The tail of the Comet always points towards the Sun.
DO YOU KNOW?
Our solar system has 08 planets, 176 moons, 05 dwarf planets and several Asteroids, comets and Meteoroids.
Halley's Comet:

Halley's Comet is comet visible from Earth every 75-76 years. Halley's Comet last appeared in 1986 and will next appear in 2061. It takes about 75 years to orbit the Sun. Edmond Halley identified it as a comet for the first time in 1758. It is the most famous comet because it marked the first time astronomers understood comets.
Halley's Comet:

Ancient people were afraid of this comet because they thought that it will bring floods and Earth quakes. Some people fear that it will hit the Earth or Moon, but with astronomical advancement we know that there is no chance of such events. Now most people are fascinated with the idea of seeing this rare astronomical event. How would you feel if you see it in the night sky?
12.5 SATELLITES

A satellite is an object that orbits around a larger object. Earth is a satellite because it orbits the Sun. The moon is a satellite which moves around Earth. There are two different types of satellites;
Natural satellites
These satellites exist naturally in the universe, for example, Earth is a planet and moon is its natural satellite.
Artificial satellites
A man-made satellite is a machine that is launched into space and orbits around a body in space, for example, Hubble Space Telescope.

Text 1A
There have been many Nabis and Rasools in history. In fact, Allah (ﷻ) sent a Rasool for every age and every nation of the world to guide the people on the right path.

Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) was the greatest and the last of all the Nabi and Rasools of Allah (ﷻ). He (ﷺ) was for all people and for all ages. There will be no Nabi or Rasool after him.
Text 1A

Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) was born on 20th April, 571 A.D. His father, Hazrat Abdullah, lived in Makkah and died a few months before the birth of his child. His grandfather, Hazrat Abdul Muttalib, named him Muhammad. His mother loved to call him Ahmad.
Text 1A

Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) was looked after by a foster-mother named Hazrat Haleema. He (ﷺ) remained with her till he (ﷺ) was five. When he (ﷺ) was six years old, his mother took Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) to the grave of his father in Madina Munawarrah. His mother died on the way back.
Text 1A
Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) now lived with his grandfather, Hazrat Abdul Muttalib who also died soon afterwards. Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) was left to the care of his uncle, Hazrat Abu Talib.
Text 1A

Since childhood, Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) was loved and respected by all. He (ﷺ) never told a lie and was called 'Sadiq'. He (ﷺ) was always honest and fair in his dealings with people. People also called him 'Amin'. A rich and noble widow of Makkah, Hazrat Khadija (رضی اللہ عنہا), was so pleased with his honesty and truthfulness that she wished to marry him. Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) accepted her proposal.
Text 1A
Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) was kind, gentle and merciful. He loved the poor. He (ﷺ) treated the orphans and the widows with kindness. He (ﷺ) helped the slaves and the helpless. His love was for all.
Text 1A
He (ﷺ) would feed the hungry even if he (ﷺ) himself had to go without food for several nights.
Text 1A

Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) had great respect for women. He (ﷺ) always remembered his mother and foster-mother with great respect. "Women are weak," he (ﷺ) said to his followers, "You should treat them with kindness and love. Their duty is to be good and modest; you should be kind to them."
Text 1A

He (ﷺ) was kind to the poor slaves. He (ﷺ) loved them as his own children. To the Muslims he (ﷺ) said, "Feed your slaves with such food as you eat yourself and clothe them with such clothes as you wear yourself. If they do wrong, pardon them. If you cannot pardon, part with them. But never treat them unkindly."
Text 1A
Hazrat Khadija (رضی اللہ عنہا) had a slave named Hazrat Zaid (رضی اللہ عنہ). Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) always treated him like his own child. He (ﷺ) always helped the needy.
Text 1A

There was an old man who used to bring water from a distant stream for his master. Hazrat Muhammad, (ﷺ) the Rasool of Allah, pitied him and helped him in carrying the water. After finishing the work he (ﷺ) said to him, "Do remember me whenever you need help again."
Text 1A
Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) used to buy and carry things of everyday use for women who could not buy or carry them themselves.

He was kind to birds and animals too. One day he (ﷺ) saw a camel driver beating his camel to go faster. Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) advised the camel driver, "Be kind to your animal. It is old and weak and the load is too heavy."

Text 1B

Abdul Sattar Edhi, often referred to as the "Angel of Mercy," was a remarkable humanitarian who dedicated his life to serving those in need. Born in 1928 in the city of Gujarat, India, his family migrated to Pakistan in 1947. Edhi's early life experiences shaped his profound compassion and unwavering commitment to the welfare of others.
Text 1B

Growing up in a family of limited means, Edhi witnessed poverty and suffering from an early age. These experiences deeply impacted him, instilling in him a strong sense of empathy and a desire to alleviate the hardships faced by the less fortunate. His personal experiences became the driving force behind his tireless efforts to bring positive change to society.
Text 1B

His mother's serious and persistent illness, and then her death created an everlasting impression on his thinking patterns and personality that drove him to make a pledge to comfort suffering humanity.
Text 1B

He had the vision of establishing welfare homes and shelters to minimize the grievances of the people who lived in misery and had no one who could provide them with the basic necessities of life. Through these shelter homes, Edhi vowed to take care of the people who were maltreated, neglected and had any sort of physical or mental disability.
Text 1B

He began his mission by establishing a free dispensary for the needy in collaboration with some community members. Edhi wanted to establish an organization that could serve multiple purposes and thus founded 'Edhi Trust'.

Mother Teresa- A Humanitarian

One of the most highly respected women in the world, Mother Teresa was internationally known for her charitable work among the victims of poverty and neglect-particularly in the slums of Calcutta (now Kolkata), India.
Mother Teresa- A Humanitarian

She was born on August 26, 1910, in Skopje, Macedonia. Her birth name was Anjeze Gonxhe Bojaxhiu. In 1928, she joined a community of nuns in Ireland called the 'Sisters of Loretto'. Weeks later she sailed to India. For the next 17 years she taught at a school in Calcutta run by the 'Sisters of Loretto'.
Mother Teresa- A Humanitarian

In 1946, Mother Teresa decided to spend her life helping the sick and the poor. She studied nursing and started working in the slums of Calcutta. In 1948, she founded the Missionaries of Charity, a religious order of women dedicated to serving the poor. Mother Teresa led the order for nearly 50 years. It opened schools for children and centres to treat the blind, the disabled, the old, and the dying.
Mother Teresa- A Humanitarian
She received many awards for her work.
Mother Teresa- A Humanitarian

The authorities greatly acknowledged her efforts. She received many titles and awards such as 'Decree of Praise', the 'Jewel of India', 'Gold Medal of the Soviet Peace Committee', and the Nobel Peace Prize for "bringing help to suffering humanity". She received honorary degrees from academic institutions worldwide and was declared a saint by the Roman Catholic Church in 2016.
Points to know!

Mother Teresa- A Humanitarian

In 1989, Mother Teresa suffered a heart attack. Despite her poor health, she continued to work in Calcutta most of the time until she retired in March, 1997. Mother Teresa worked day and night to achieve her goal by ignoring her health. She suffered another heart attack and died on September 5, 1997, at the age of 87. After her death, the Missionaries of Charity carried on her work in more than 90 countries.
Mother Teresa- A Humanitarian

Mother Teresa will be remembered for showing compassion and helping 'the unwanted, and the uncared for'. A pronoun is a word that stands in place of a noun. There are different types of pronouns.
Use of Language

Personal pronouns are used in place of the person, place or thing that we are talking about. We can use personal pronouns as a subject and as an object of a sentence. Personal pronouns are also used to show possession or ownership. Their form changes to indicate a person, number, gender, or case.

Text 1D

Helen Keller (1880-1968) was an author, an activist and a campaigner for the charities for deaf and blind. Helen became deaf and blind as a young child and had to struggle to overcome her dual disability. However, she became the first deaf-blind person to attain a bachelor's degree and an influential campaigner for disability issues.
Text 1D
Her public profile helped destigmatise blindness and deafness, and she was seen as a powerful example of someone overcoming difficult circumstances.
Helen Keller-A Girl with a Vision

Helen Adams Keller was born on June 27, 1880, in Tuscumbia, Alabama. When she was 19 months old, she got very sick. The disease left her unable to see or hear. Her parents remained optimistic and took her to the famous inventor Alexander Graham Bell who helped her find a good teacher.
Helen Keller-A Girl with a Vision

When Helen was 6, she got a teacher named Anne Sullivan. Sullivan used Helen's sense of touch to teach her. She handed Helen a doll and traced the letters of the word 'doll' on the palm of Helen's hand. With Sullivan's help, Helen made rapid progress. Soon she could read sentences by feeling raised words on cardboard.
Helen Keller-A Girl with a Vision

She went to a school for the deaf in Boston. Here, she learned that she could use her hands to teach herself how to use Braille. Then she used a Braille typewriter to type out stories of her own. She also spent the next twenty-five years of her life learning to speak so that others could understand her. Learning to speak was a bigger challenge.
Helen Keller-A Girl with a Vision

Helen did it by touching the lips and throat of a person who was speaking. She was able to feel the way the lips moved and the throat vibrated. At the same time someone spelled out the words that were being spoken.
Helen Keller-A Girl with a Vision
Keller was very bright. She graduated from Radcliffe College in 1904. Then she wrote magazine articles that told people about blindness. She also wrote several books about her life.
Helen Keller-A Girl with a Vision
In 1913 Keller began lecturing—with the aid of an interpreter—worldwide on the needs of the blind. She spoke primarily on behalf of the Foundation for the Blind, for which she raised funds.
Helen Keller-A Girl with a Vision
In 1920, Keller started her campaign to bring improvement in the life of the deaf and blind. She also prompted the organisation of commissions for the blind in 30 U.S. states by 1937.
Helen Keller-A Girl with a Vision

Besides giving lectures, Keller was a prolific writer during her lifetime. Her books include 'The Story of My Life' and 'Optimism' (both 1903), 'The World I Live In (1908)', 'Out of the Dark (1913)', 'Midstream: My Later Life' (1929), 'Helen Keller's Journal' (1938), and 'Let Us Have Faith' (1940).
Helen Keller-A Girl with a Vision

Keller died in Westport, Connecticut, on June 1, 1968. Although her own life was one of silence and darkness, Helen Keller was courageous and determined enough to bring light to others by encouraging them to never give up.

Folktales are a kind of story that gets passed on from generation to generation. True folktales do not have a single author. They develop as different people tell them over time. Once upon a time there lived a crow. She had built her nest in a tree. At the root of the same tree, a snake had built its home. Whenever the crow laid eggs, the snake would eat them up. The crow felt helpless. "That evil snake! I must do something. Let me go and talk to him," thought the crow.

Learning first aid is an invaluable life-skill. It helps children become aware of risks and equip them with skills to keep themselves safe. They can help themselves or others if involved in a medical emergency. It could save their lives.
Text 3A

It is important to understand that first aid varies from injury to injury. If, someone has burnt their skin, you cannot apply the same procedure required for bleeding. Some of the first aid procedures are given below for your understanding.
First Aid — What to do if Someone has a Burn

1. If somebody has been burnt by something hot, the most important thing is to cool down the burnt area using water. • 2. Do not remove anything that is stuck to the burn. • 3. Very carefully remove any loose clothing which is covering the burn. Put on gloves if possible. • 4. Next, put their burn under cool running water (you could use a tap or a hose). • 5.
First Aid — What to do if Someone has a Burn

Then, hold the burn under the water for a full 15 to 20 minutes. Avoid applying ice to burned tissue. It can cause more damage. • 6. If the burn is really big and painful, you need to call Rescue 1122. Always tell an adult what happened and get burns seen by a health professional.
Points to Know!

When you provide basic medical care to someone experiencing a sudden injury or illness, it's known as first aid. In some cases, first aid consists of the initial support provided to someone in the middle of a medical emergency. This support might help them survive until professional help arrives.
First Aid — How to help someone with a heatstroke
1. When your body overheats, it can cause heat exhaustion. If left untreated, heat exhaustion can lead to heatstroke. This is a potentially life-threatening condition and medical emergency.
First Aid — How to help someone with a heatstroke
If someone is overheated, encourage them to rest in a cool location. Remove excess layers of clothing and try to cool their body down by doing the following:
First Aid — How to help someone with a heatstroke
Cover them with a cool, damp sheet. • Apply a cool, wet towel to the back of their neck. • Sponge them with cool water.
First Aid — How to help someone with a heatstroke
2. If someone with heatstroke, gets fever, or gets unconscious, call Rescue 1122 for help or seek immediate medical attention.
Preventive Measures to avoid heatstrokes:

Some parts of Pakistan are extremely hot and the temperature can rise up to 50 degrees. You need to stay careful in these hot weather conditions. Some of the things you can do to prevent heatstrokes are:
Preventive Measures to avoid heatstrokes:
Stay in a cool place when the heat index climbs • Stay hydrated when it's hot outside. • Drink plenty of water and juices. • Take a bath or a shower twice a day.
First Aid — How to Treat someone with a Nosebleed
To treat someone with a nosebleed, ask them to:
First Aid — How to Treat someone with a Nosebleed

1. Sit down and lean their head forward. • 2. Using the thumb and index finger, firmly press or pinch the nostrils closed. • 3. Continue to apply this pressure continuously for five minutes. • 4. Check and repeat until the bleeding stops.
First Aid — How to Treat someone with a Nosebleed
If the nosebleed continues for 20 minutes or longer, seek emergency medical care. Call Rescue 1122 for help.

The Modern Olympics

The Olympic Games, the biggest international sporting event, has a rich history dating back to ancient Greece. However, the modern Olympics, as we know them today, began in 1896. The driving force behind the revival of the games was Pierre de Coubertin, a visionary French educator. The Modern Olympics

The Olympic Games have grown exponentially in both scale and popularity. Today, they are held every four years, alternating between the Summer Olympics and the Winter Olympics. Athletes from across the globe train diligently to qualify for this prestigious event, showcasing their skills and striving for personal and national glory.

The Olympic torch represents the perpetual spirit of the games. The torch relay, carried out by a succession of runners, signifies the passing of this sacred flame from one generation to the next.

Simple Sentences
A sentence is commonly defined as "a complete unit of thought." A simple sentence is the simplest form of a sentence that has only one independent main clause. It conveys a complete meaning.
Simple Sentences

The basic parts of a sentence are the subject and the verb. The subject is usually a noun—a word (or phrase) that names a person, place, or thing. The verb (or predicate) usually follows the subject and identifies an action or a state of being.
Simple Sentences
Example: The Olympics (subject) were organised (verb).
Points to know!
The predicate tells us about the subject. It always includes the main verb.
Simple Sentences
There are a variety of simple sentences.
Subject Predicate
A simple sentence can also be divided into two parts to make learning easier. These are the subject and the predicate. Example: He (subject) experimented by moving the patient gently. (predicate)
Subject Verb
A simple sentence may have only a subject and a verb. Example: I (subject) played. (verb)
Subject Intransitive Verb

The S–IV pattern is the simplest sentence type. It includes a subject and an intransitive verb. Example: He (subject) jumped (intransitive verb). The athlete listens. The ring shines. The flower blossomed.
Points to know!
Intransitive verbs do not have a direct object.
Subject, Verb and Adverb
A simple sentence sometimes has a subject, a verb and an adverb. Examples: The athletes (subject) run. (verb) — Pierre De Coubertin (subject) listens. (verb)
Subject, Verb and Adverb

Note that the action verbs in the examples, run and listens, can stand alone. They may be accompanied by modifiers, too. Example: The camera battery (subject) could have died (verb) suddenly. (adverb) — Audience (subject) could laugh (verb) at the joke. (adverb)

Birth & family: Date of Birth: 31 July 1893 · Date of Death: 9 July 1967 (aged 73) · Place of Birth: Karachi · Father's Name: Jinnahbhai Poonja · Mother's Name: Mithibai Jinnah
Mohtarma Fatima Jinnah

Education: Fatima Jinnah received her primary and secondary education from Bandra Convent in Bombay. Later, she pursued her medical degree in Dentistry from Dr. R. Ahmed Dental College, University of Calcutta.
Mohtarma Fatima Jinnah
Occupation: Fatima Jinnah was a dental surgeon by profession. She established her dental clinic in Bombay in 1923. Later, she wound up her dental practise in 1929 to take active part in politics.
Mohtarma Fatima Jinnah

Achievements and Contributions: Mohtarma Fatima Jinnah earned the title of 'Madar-e-Millat' (Mother of the Nation) due to her untiring efforts for the people of Pakistan. She was involved in all political activities side by side with her brother Muhammad Ali Jinnah (the founder of Pakistan). Fatima Jinnah was the member of the working committee of Bombay Provincial Muslim League.
Mohtarma Fatima Jinnah

In March 1940 she attended the Lahore resolution of the Muslims League. It was primarily due to her initiative that the All India Muslim Women Students Federation was organised in February 1941 in Delhi. During the transfer of power in 1947, Jinnah formed the 'Women's Relief Committee', which played a significant role in the settlement of Muhajirs in the new state of Pakistan.

Phrasal Verbs

A phrasal verb is a combination of words (a verb + a preposition or verb +adverb) that when used together, usually take on a different meaning to that of the original verb. For example, 'goes' means 'moves' –as in 'The train goes west.' But when you add the word 'out' with it, the meaning changes. For example, 'goes out' –as in 'The light goes out.'

Text 6A

Some people have strangest of jobs in the world and they love them. It is very important to love what you are doing; no matter what. Given below is information on some of the coolest jobs in the world. Skim and scan the text for information. Do you wish to pursue any of these jobs?
Strangest Jobs in the World
Have you ever thought that caring for animals could be a very well-paid job. If not, the passage below may change your perspective.
Wildlife Photographer

This job is all about taking photos of wild animals in their natural habitats. But a wildlife photographer also needs knowledge about the animals. Not only do they have to photograph well, they need to have an understanding of the landscapes in which they live. A wildlife photographer needs to venture into remote locations and take beautiful photos of the animals even in the most dangerous spots.
Wildlife Photographer

Wildlife photographers need to be prepared for long journeys, since many of these animals live in remote places or dark forests. They have to carry heavy equipment so they have to exercise a lot. Patience is another characteristic required by wildlife photographers. Sometimes, it can take hours (or days) to get just the right shot.
Wildlife Photographer
*Wildlife photographers sometimes, need to camouflage themselves, so the animals cannot spot them.*
Strangest Jobs in the World
People who want to become wildlife photographers need to start photographing creatures close to home first, like birds, bugs or even stray animals.
LegoLand Model Maker

Spend your days building a world out of LEGO bricks. There are LEGOLAND resorts around the world and all of them require a team of people to maintain the models and create new displays for big events. With just bricks and their brains, model makers come up with the designs and then put them together for the public to enjoy.
LegoLand Model Maker

When you interview for this job, you'll be entered into a 'brick-off' building challenge against other applicants, so practice with those blocks. They need some creative design experience for imagining all the model ideas, as well as knowledge of maths and science for planning out how to actually construct those huge models so they don't topple over.
Strangest Jobs in the World

Legoland Windsor offers you the chance to work with a Master Builder for a day. You can begin by building a figure of yourself or any other thing. They teach you the techniques to created various themed models and go behind the scenes at the resort.
Sand Sculptor

Make sandcastles for a living. This job seems pretty straightforward-just create amazing models out of sand and water. But its harder than it looks to become the best and get paid for it! There are only 300 master sand sculptors in the world. To win the World Championships of sand sculpting or become a Guinness World Record holder can take years of handwork and training.
Sand Sculptor

Sand sculptors can make their money by winning competitions. They usually have less than 24 hours to complete their models. Once a sculptor has built a reputation, they may also hired to sculpt at events. Sand can be brought to any location and sculpted into something linked to a brand or event.
Sand Sculptor
An airline once paid for sculptors to create sand passengers jetting to a beach destination as part of its marketing campaign!
Hot Air Balloon Pilot

A job that allows you to be on cloud nine. As a commercial balloon pilot, you'll fly sky high, feeling as free as a bird-and get paid to take others with you. A hot air balloon pilot might take part in competitions, fly tourists around or display advertisements on your balloon, but on every trip you'll find moments of calm as you quietly drift along with the wind.
Hot Air Balloon Pilot

To qualify for the job, you'll need to attend hot air balloon school. The first requirement is to obtain your private pilot's license, then your balloon certificate, after which you can train with a commercial instructor. You might be lucky to complete this within three months, but if you want to fly above certain heights you'll need more experience.
Hot Air Balloon Pilot
You need to master a smooth landing if you want to keep your passengers happy, too!
Hot Air Balloon Pilot
In our modern-day busy skies, you'll always need to check airspace restrictions, flight rules and emergency procedures. This job is suitable for people who are skilled at working methodically.

Maintaining a Journal/Diary:
Given below is a how a typical day looks like in the life of an astronaut.
6 am:

I woke up by an alarm in my small sleep station. It's time to float out of the sleeping bag and brush my teeth- which is a little different when in zero gravity. I have to swallow the paste when I am done.
8 am:

It's time to put in a call to mission control to discuss the day's schedule. There are household chores and maintenance jobs to do. All the tasks have been carefully written down step-by-step but the team at mission control. I have to be careful not to lose things. Everything needs to be secured to the walls or it will float away.
10 am:
Hit the gym for two hours. Zero gravity affects the bones and I'll lose muscle strength because I move so effortlessly, so the gym is a requirement, not a choice.

I worked on my schedule, attended a meeting with team members on the Earth. Had my food alone. Eating in space means adding hot water to the dehydrated packet of food to make it edible. It's not really very nice but my options in space are limited.
2 pm:

The main reason I've been sent to live in space is to conduct scientific research so I worked on my experiments in the lab throughout the afternoon. I studied the effects of zero gravity on materials and on the living creatures like the fish and ant, I brought on board with me.
8 pm:
After dinner, I had plenty of free time to call home or watch a movie. I did both. Sometimes, I spend my time looking down on planet Earth as well before snuggling down to sleep.
Text 6B

The reading passage is taken from the novel, "A Man Called Ove," written by Fredrik Backman: This famous novel revolves around Ove, a grumpy and isolated man who finds unexpected friendship and purpose by helping others.
A Man Called Ove

Ove was a man of strict routines and firm principles. Every morning, without fail, he would wake up at precisely 6:00 a.m., put on his worn-out slippers, and shuffle to the kitchen. He would boil water for his tea, carefully select a slice of bread, and spread it with just the right amount of butter and jam. This simple ritual gave him a sense of control and order in his otherwise mundane life.
A Man Called Ove

Living in a neat row of houses, Ove was known by his neighbours as the grumpy old man with a perpetual scowl on his face. He had a reputation for complaining about everything—from the noisy children playing outside to the improper parking of cars. Ove liked to keep his surroundings in perfect order and didn't appreciate any disruption to his carefully maintained peace.
A Man Called Ove

But there was much more to Ove than met the eye. Behind his gruff exterior lay a heart that yearned for connection and understanding. He had experienced great loss in his life, losing his beloved wife Sonja, and his grief had hardened him. Ove had built emotional walls to protect himself, leading others to perceive him as a cantankerous old soul.
A Man Called Ove

One fateful day, a new family moved into the house next door. They were a lively bunch, with two young children and their parents. Ove was immediately irked by the noise they made and the chaos that seemed to follow them wherever they went. Their belongings were scattered all over their front yard, disrupting the harmony of the neighbourhood.
While reading
Why do you think Ove was so unhappy all the time?
A Man Called Ove

Despite his initial resistance, Ove found himself unexpectedly drawn to the family. The children, with their wide-eyed curiosity and innocence, saw beyond Ove's grumpiness. They waved and smiled at him every time they spotted him, undeterred by his stern countenance. Slowly but surely, Ove's defences began to soften.
A Man Called Ove

One day, he noticed that the family's bicycle had a flat tyre. Against his better judgment, Ove offered to help fix it. As he worked on the bicycle, he discovered a sense of purpose and satisfaction he had long forgotten. The children watched in awe as Ove skillfully repaired the tyre, their faces beaming with gratitude.
A Man Called Ove

From that day forward, Ove became an integral part of the neighbourhood. He became the go-to person for handyman tasks, fixing broken appliances and repairing fences. The neighbours soon realized that beneath Ove's gruff exterior was a man with a compassionate heart and a wealth of knowledge.
A Man Called Ove

Ove's transformation extended beyond his acts of service. He developed genuine friendships with his neighbours, forming bonds that transcended the superficial barriers of age and background. Ove discovered that life could be meaningful even in the simplest acts of kindness and connection.
A Man Called Ove

The story of Ove teaches us an important lesson about the power of compassion and understanding. It reminds us that there is often more to a person than meets the eye and that we should never judge someone solely based on appearances or first impressions. Ove's journey illustrates the profound impact kindness and empathy can have on both individuals and communities.
A Man Called Ove

*Fredrik Backman is a Swedish author known for his heartfelt and engaging novels. He was born on June 2, 1981, in Stockholm, Sweden. 'A Man Called Ove' is his debut novel which gained him popularity and recognition.*

A gerund is a noun formed from a verb. All gerunds end in -ing. As they are nouns, gerunds can function as one of the following:
Use of Language
The Subject of a Verb. Example: The labouring hours suit my spirit. ('labouring' is the subject of the verb 'suit')
Use of Language
The Object of a Verb. Example: I enjoy traveling the market-place. ("traveling" is the direct object of the verb "enjoy.")
Use of Language
The Object of a Preposition Example: I surprised them by working in the field and in the forest. ("working" is the object of the preposition "by.")
Use of Language

A Subject Complement Example: My favourite was visiting the tranquil room. ("Visiting" is a subject complement. It completes the linking verb "was" and renames the subject, making it a subject complement.)

Figurative Language:

Simile: A simile is a particular way of using language to have an effect on readers. It makes a comparison between something in common. Similes use 'like' or as to make the comparison. For example, as cold as ice, as light as a feather and as cool as a cucumber etc.
Figurative Language:

Metaphor: A metaphor is another example of using language that makes a comparison. It is more direct than a simile. Metaphors help to make your writing creatively rich. For example, He is a lion when he comes to the field or My mom has a heart of gold.
Figurative Language:

Personification: Personification is a type of metaphor that presents non-human thing as if it is a person. Poets and writers use metaphors and personification to help readers to think about things in a new or different way. For example, The tree was tall could be The tree stretched its arms towards the sky. Example: Sunshine (not a person) tiptoed through my window (behaving like a person).
Figurative Language:
Poems often contain imagery. Imagery is the pictures or feelings that are created in your mind. Poets use figurative language to create images in various ways:
Daffodils

I wandered lonely as a cloud / That floats on high o'er vales and hills, / When all at once I saw a crowd, / A host, of golden daffodils; / Beside the lake, beneath the trees, / Fluttering and dancing in the breeze.
Daffodils

Continuous as the stars that shine / And twinkle on the milky way, / They stretched in never-ending line / Along the margin of a bay: / Ten thousand saw I at a glance, / Tossing their heads in sprightly dance.
Daffodils

The waves beside them danced, but they / Out-did the sparkling waves in glee: / A poet could not be but gay, / In such a jocund company: / I gazed—and gazed—but little thought / What wealth the show to me had brought:
Daffodils

For oft, when on my couch I lie / In vacant or in pensive mood, / They flash upon that inward eye / Which is the bliss of solitude; / And then my heart with pleasure fills, / And dances with the daffodils. (William Wordsworth)

Text 7B

"Curiosity is the key to problem solving."-Galileo Galilei. He loved to invent things. He made a telescope that lets him see as far as other planets. His ideas changed the way scientists worked and he is considered to be the world's most famous astronomer.
Galileo Galilei, the Father of Modern Science

Galileo was a brilliant mathematician and astronomer. His scientific observations and inventions changed the way people thought about the world. His ideas and discoveries are still relevant today. One of the most important scientists in history, Galileo Galilei was born in Pisa, Italy in 1564. He came from a large family, being the oldest of six children.
Galileo Galilei, the Father of Modern Science

His family moved to Florence when he was eight but he stayed in Pisa and went to school at a monastery. This is a place where monks live, work and pray. Having been educated by monks, Galileo thought about becoming a priest but he chose a different direction.
Galileo Galilei, the Father of Modern Science
He started to study medicine in order to become a doctor but he was naturally curious about the world and space, but chose to become an astronomer and a scientist.
Galileo Galilei, the Father of Modern Science

He used Mathematics to become a very successful scientist. He invented a telescope that was much better than anyone had made before. This meant that he was able to spot objects around distant planets. He was the first to see Moons orbiting Jupiter. These Moons are known as the 'Galilean Satellites' after Galileo. He was a frequent inventor, making telescopes, thermometers and a new kind of compass.
Galileo Galilei, the Father of Modern Science

He had some ideas that made him unpopular because they were different to what other people believed. When looking at Jupiter, he saw four objects orbiting the planet. He announced that they were moons but most people didn't believe him as they believed they were stars. He believed that those are moons travelling around Jupiter as they disappeared regularly and stars do not disappear.
Galileo Galilei, the Father of Modern Science

Perhaps his most important idea was that the Earth went around the Sun, as did the other planets. Many people disagreed with him, arguing it was the Sun that went around the Earth but he was proven to be correct by later scientists.
Galileo Galilei, the Father of Modern Science
Galileo pioneered the use of the telescope for observing the night sky. His discoveries undermined traditional ideas about the perfect and unchanging cosmos with the Earth as its centre.
The Tower of Pisa Experiment

At that time, it was believed that if two objects were dropped from the same height, the heavier one would land first. To test this, Galileo went to the top of the Leaning Tower of Pisa and dropped two balls of different weights. They both landed at the same time. He had disproved the original theory.
Use of Language

Prepositional phrase is a modifying phrase consisting of a preposition and its object. Prepositional phrases modify nouns and verbs while indicating various relationships between subjects and verbs. A prepositional phrase starts with a preposition and ends with a noun or pronoun. Example: Galileo thought about becoming a priest but he chose a different direction.
